Care about your craft and think critically about every decision in real time rather than running on autopilot.

Choose tools, languages, and approaches by their fit to the specific circumstances rather than committing to a single best technology, and keep a broad computer-science grounding and wide practical experience so you can choose well; the core techniques are universal across code, design, docs, and teams.

Continuously invest small daily effort in a diversified, regularly rebalanced knowledge portfolio (learn new languages and read widely, learn emerging tech early, broaden beyond your stack), treating your knowledge as an expiring asset.
Critically analyze what you read and hear so your knowledge stays accurate and free of vendor or media hype.

Take responsibility for your work; when you err, admit it and provide options to salvage the situation rather than excuses or blame, and anticipate uncontrolled risks with contingency plans while rehearsing bad news with concrete alternatives.
Do not live with broken windows: fix bad designs, wrong decisions, and poor code as soon as they are found, or board them up, because neglect and the broken-window effect accelerate software rot.

Be a catalyst for change by building something reasonable and demonstrable when you cannot get approval for the whole, and keep the big picture in view, since most disasters and overruns accumulate gradually.
Make quality an explicit requirements issue and involve users in the trade-off; deliver good software early for feedback rather than chasing perfection, and know when to stop refining.

Communicate effectively as a core professional skill: plan what to say, know and tailor to your audience, choose the moment and style, mind presentation, make it two-way, and treat email as permanent.

Apply DRY: every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system, because duplicated knowledge guarantees eventual inconsistency, and maintenance is continuous throughout development.

Eliminate duplication by generating all derived forms from one authoritative source with an active code generator wired into the build, normalizing data, using calculated fields, accessor functions, and generating tests from the specification; keep simple input formats and remember generators need not produce code.
Make finding and reusing existing code easier than rewriting it, and prevent interdeveloper duplication with clear design, frequent communication, a project librarian, and shared utilities.
You may deliberately break DRY for performance, such as caching, but localize the violation behind the owning module's interface.
Resist impatient copy-paste duplication under deadline pressure, because shortcuts taken now cost more later.

Design orthogonal, decoupled components that each have a single, well-defined responsibility, to gain productivity (localized change, M-by-N reuse) and reduce risk (isolation, less fragility); eliminate effects between unrelated things.

Keep systems orthogonal with layering, an orthogonality test (a single requirement change should affect one module), and isolation of third-party tools behind abstract interfaces; do not rely on properties of things you cannot control.
Recognize that nonorthogonal systems have no local fix, and use the difficulty of building a module's unit test as a probe for poor decoupling.

Write shy code and obey the Law of Demeter (call methods only on objects you own, were passed, or created, and ask the owning object for what you need) to minimize coupling, because larger response sets are empirically more error-prone.
Balance the Law of Demeter against its wrapper-method overhead, reversing it to tightly couple modules only for a well-known, acceptable performance trade-off.
Avoid global data and near-identical functions (refactor them via patterns such as Strategy), since both increase coupling.
Make logical and physical design proceed in tandem, avoiding cyclic dependencies among files, directories, and libraries, which are extremely hard to undo.

Organize teams orthogonally around functionality rather than job functions, with cohesive self-contained groups, no siloed phases, and two heads (one technical, one administrative) for responsible self-direction.

Treat decisions as reversible: abstract third-party products behind interfaces, treat the deployment model as configuration, maintain flexibility in architecture and vendor integration, and keep change-injection mechanisms reversible, because anything you rely on heavily will change.

Treat software as gardening and refactor early and often (when you find duplication, nonorthogonality, drift, or a performance need), taking short, tested steps without adding functionality at the same time and breaking the build on incompatible interface changes.
Configure, don't integrate: drive deeply ingrained choices and volatile business rules from metadata kept in plain text, putting abstractions in the code and details outside the compiled code base.
Prefer programs that can reload their configuration while running for long-lived processes, weighing the added complexity.

Use tracer bullets (a thin, production-quality, end-to-end skeleton fleshed out incrementally) to find the target under uncertainty, adjusting aim from early misses; tracer code is lean but complete, not a throwaway prototype.

Prototype to learn: build cheap, disposable prototypes (even non-code) of anything risky, ignoring inessential details and using a high-level language, set disposability expectations clearly, and switch to tracer bullets if the prototype may be mistaken for a deliverable.

Do not be a slave to formal methods or expensive tools: fit techniques to your team's practices, prefer prototypes users can actually check, account for the real cost of adopting new methods, and remember expensive tools do not produce better designs.

Program close to the problem domain using its vocabulary (backed by a glossary) and mini-languages, which enable domain-specific validation and can serve each class of user; a mini-language can grow from a non-executable specification into executable code, and embedding it lets behavior change without recompiling.

Estimate to avoid surprises: match accuracy and units to context, build and decompose a model, focus on high-impact parameters, beware estimates built on sub-estimates, record and learn from estimates, and ask someone who has done it before.
Iterate the schedule with the code through incremental development, and answer on-the-spot estimate requests with a commitment to get back to them after working the steps.
Estimate the order of your algorithms from their structure and address bad orders with divide-and-conquer, but choose algorithms pragmatically since the asymptotically fastest is not always best.
Test your estimates against production reality (plotting runs and profiling) and avoid premature optimization until a bottleneck is confirmed.

Keep knowledge in human-readable plain text, which is self-describing, tool-friendly, and outlives the applications that created it; binary formats are no more secure, so encrypt or checksum sensitive values instead.
Master your basic tools, since tools amplify talent: treat the command shell as a workbench, know one editor deeply and use it everywhere, and do not confine yourself to a single IDE.

Always use source code control for everything, even solo or throwaway work, because it is a project-wide time machine that enables change tracking, branching, concurrent work, and automatic repeatable builds.

Do not use manual procedures; automate everything the team does (builds, tests, web publishing, administrivia) with scripted, repeatable tools kept under source control and scheduling, and let the computer do the repetitious, mundane work.
Learn a text-manipulation language and write code that writes code, because both multiply your productivity at a one-time cost.
Treat debugging as blame-free problem solving: do not panic, fix the root cause rather than the symptom, and start from cleanly compiling, warning-free code.

Gather accurate debugging data: reproduce a bug with a single command, observe accurately (interview the reporter), visualize the data, use consistent tracing, and inspect memory around a corrupt variable.

Assume a bug is in your own code rather than the OS, compiler, or library, and that a single recent change is the likely cause; do not assume but prove it in context, and after a surprising bug strengthen the tests so it cannot recur.
Retest the whole system after upgrading third-party software such as the OS, compiler, or database, weighing the timing of the upgrade.
Accept that you cannot write perfect software and code defensively, validating inputs and distrusting even your own code.

Design with contracts: specify each routine's preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants, keep contracts abstract, be strict in what you accept and promise as little as possible, and do not use preconditions for user-input validation.

Honor the Liskov Substitution Principle and put a contract once in the base class so subtypes preserve method meaning; recognize that assertions only partially emulate Design by Contract, so prefer languages or tools with real DBC support.
Crash early: treat every error as information, and when something impossible happens terminate the program promptly, because a dead program does far less damage than a crippled one.
Use assertions to guard conditions that should never happen, keep their evaluation side-effect-free, leave them on in production, and never substitute them for real error handling.

Use exceptions only for exceptional problems (verify by checking whether the code would still run with all handlers removed) to keep error handling in one place; do not use them in normal flow, where they create spaghetti and break encapsulation, and consider error handlers as an alternative.
Use loop and semantic invariants to pin boundary conditions and inviolate requirements, and design a piece of software's contract whenever you design the software.

Finish what you start: the routine or object that allocates a resource frees it; free on every exit path, nest allocations (free in reverse order, acquire in a consistent order to avoid deadlock), encapsulate resources, avoid global handles, and verify resources are actually freed.
Treat time, both concurrency and ordering, as a design element: analyze workflow to find parallelism and decouple time and order dependencies for flexibility.
Design using independent, concurrent services behind well-defined, consistent interfaces, communicating through asynchronous work queues and using a hungry-consumer model for load balancing.
Always design for concurrency: protect shared and global state, keep objects in a valid state whenever they could be called, and avoid hidden inter-call state for cleaner, thread-safe interfaces.
Separate views from models (Model-View-Controller as a general technique), use events and publish/subscribe so senders need no knowledge of receivers, and build model-viewer networks for flexibility.

Use a blackboard combined with a rules engine to coordinate workflow among anonymous, asynchronous, heterogeneous participants, especially when data arrives in unpredictable order or feedback is involved, and partition the blackboard as it grows.

Program deliberately, not by coincidence: rely only on documented, reliable behavior, do not depend on unguaranteed context, remove spurious calls, and document and test your assumptions, because coding is design work that demands thought.

Design to test: design each module's contract and its tests together and write the tests before the code, test against the contract over boundary conditions, and test subcomponents before the modules that depend on them.

Make tests easy to find and ship them with the code, run them often, build a composable test harness (reusing a framework such as xUnit), formalize ad hoc tests into the suite, and build a test window into deployed software; internal test drivers are worth building even when no requirement asks for them, and tests should return exit codes so they compose.

Test state coverage rather than mere code coverage, using both real and synthetic data, decoupling application logic from the GUI, analyzing design metrics comparatively across modules, and using saboteurs to verify the tests actually catch bugs.
Do not use wizard-generated or any code you do not understand, because it becomes interwoven with your own code and you must be able to maintain and debug it.
Dig for requirements rather than gather them, discover the underlying reason a user does something, and work alongside a user to think like one.

Separate requirements (need) from policy and architecture and keep requirements abstract without overspecifying: capture semantic invariants as requirements, restate fixed values as configurability, and translate surface behaviors into underlying needs.

Invest in abstractions over details because abstractions live longer, capture requirements as abstract use cases without being a slave to any notation, and maintain a shared project glossary and hyperlinked documentation.

Avoid the specification trap: some things are better done than described, reserve detailed specifications for life-critical systems or shared interfaces, and treat requirements, design, and implementation as one feedback-driven process.
Manage requirements creep by actively tracking requirements and showing sponsors each new feature's impact on the schedule.
Solve hard problems by finding the real constraints and the degrees of freedom you actually have, enumerating and disproving every avenue, and asking whether and why the thing must be done at all.
Start when you are ready by heeding nagging doubts, and distinguish good judgment from procrastination by prototyping the doubtful area as a proof of concept.
Run a full nightly build that executes all available tests so regressions are caught close to their cause, and be wary of recursive make's dependency blind spots.

Test early, test often, and test automatically (with results interpreted automatically), writing test code at the same time as or before the production code, because coding is not done until all the tests run.

Cover the major testing types: unit testing as the foundation, integration testing of contracts (often the single largest source of bugs), validation and verification against the real need, resource-exhaustion and graceful-failure testing, performance and load testing, and usability testing with real users.
Find bugs once: when a bug is found, add an automated test so that a human never has to find that same bug again.

Treat documentation as code (English as another programming language) and build it in rather than bolt it on: it mirrors the code, so comment why not how, choose meaningful and non-misleading names, keep tool-maintained information out of comments, record authorship, and use executable documents with a single presentation-independent source.
Measure project success by how well it meets users' expectations: communicate expectations throughout development, then gently exceed them with low-cost delight without breaking the system.
Sign your work: take pride and responsibility in what you build, keeping code owned individually or communally with supporting practices.

Treat quality as a team issue with no broken windows and every member contributing, keep the team vigilant against creeping change, communicate to the outside as one voice, and give each member room to shine.

Apply defensive coding idioms: never use gets(), do not rely on overlapping-string strcpy, set pointers and object references to null after freeing to catch reuse and aid garbage collection, check the runtime environment dynamically, and do not bury user interaction in a library routine.

Reduce coupling and improve structure with concrete refactorings: forward-declare in headers instead of including full headers, replace type-code switches with subclasses, prefer delegation (has-a) over inheritance (is-a), and replace polling reports with listener or observer designs.

Choose error handling by how exceptional a condition is and reduce recursion footprint by sharing one buffer across calls; recognize that object technology can be more orthogonal but is easier to abuse, and modeless designs tend to be more orthogonal than modal ones.
